This page goes with **Chapter 17, Secondary Dominant Chords** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SecondaryDominants.html). Read each section there
first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It builds on [Chapter 7, Roman Numerals](roman-numerals.qmd),
[Chapter 8, Seventh Chords](seventh-chords.qmd) and [Chapter 9, Harmonic Progression](progressions.qmd).

Every drill has **Settings**, and is also on the [Theory Drills](theory-drills.qmd) page. **▶ Hear it** plays the chord and then the
chord it resolves to.

**Typing a secondary dominant:** `V/V`, `V7/ii`, `V7/IV`. After the slash comes the chord being tonicized, and its case is its quality,
as before: `ii` is minor, `IV` is major. Inversions use the figured-bass numbers the book uses: `V6/vi` and `V64/V` for triads, `V65/V`,
`V43/IV` and `V42/ii` for seventh chords. `V6/5/V` and `V7 of ii` work too.

## 17.1 Examples

Secondary dominants are everywhere, in popular and classical music. Here are the book's examples. Listen for the chord that sounds
"borrowed" from another key. Its chromatic note pulls toward the next chord. The rest of the chapter explains what it is.
[Read 17.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ExamplesWithSecondaryDominants.html)

## 17.2 Tonicization

**Tonicization** treats a chord other than I as if it were a tonic for a moment, by putting its own dominant in front of it. That
dominant is a **secondary dominant**: a major triad or a dominant seventh chord whose root is a **perfect 5th above** the root of the chord it
resolves to. It is written **V/x**, said "V of x". In C major, D–F♯–A goes to G, the V chord, so it is **V/V**. D7 is **V7/V**.
[Read 17.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Tonicization.html)

Why not call D major "II" in C? Because ii in a major key is minor. A major chord on 2 is chromatic, and calling it V/V says what it
does: it leads to V. **Diminished chords are never tonicized** (vii° in major, ii° and vii° in minor), because a diminished chord cannot
sound like a tonic.

Start with triads in C, G and F major. Which chord is it?

<div class="drill" data-ex="secsym" data-settings="mode=major&most=1&kind=tri&dir=find"></div>

## 17.3 Secondary dominants in major and minor

Both kinds work as secondary dominants: the **major triad** and the **dominant (major–minor) seventh chord**. Usually the chromatic note is
**raised**. It is the leading tone of the chord being tonicized. The exception in major is **V7/IV**: its seventh is **lowered** (B♭ in
C major), the way the last flat added to a key signature is 4̂ of the new key.
[Read 17.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SecondaryDominantsInMajorAndMinor.html)

| C major: tonicized | V/x | V7/x | C minor: tonicized | V/x | V7/x |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ii (Dm) | A | A7 | ii° (D°) | none | none |
| iii (Em) | B | B7 | III (E♭) | B♭ (= VII) | B♭7 (= VII7) |
| IV (F) | C (= I) | C7 | iv (Fm) | C | C7 |
| V (G) | D | D7 | V (G) | D | D7 |
| vi (Am) | E | E7 | VI (A♭) | E♭ (= III) | E♭7 |
| vii° (B°) | none | none | VII (B♭) | F | F7 |

The chords marked "=" use only notes of the key, so on their own they look like ordinary diatonic chords. Only what follows them shows
that they are secondary dominants. The drills leave them out. The book points out one more case: in minor, F major before B♭ is V/VII,
but before G (or B°) it is IV.

## 17.4 Analysing secondary dominants

The book's two steps for a chord with a chromatic note:

1. **Stack it in thirds** to find the root and the quality. If it isn't a major triad or a dominant seventh, it isn't a secondary dominant.
2. **Go down a perfect 5th** from the root. If that note is the root of a major or minor chord in the key, the chord is V (or V7) of
   that chord.

The chord on the staff is followed by the chord it tonicizes. Name the first one:

[Read 17.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/AnalyzingSecondaryDominants.html)

<div class="drill" data-ex="secdom" data-settings="mode=major&most=3&kind=both&inv=root&clef=treble,bass"></div>

With inversions. The book's example is an F♯ major triad in first inversion. B, a perfect 5th below F♯, is 5̂ of the key, so the
chord is **V6/V**. Read the bass note to choose the figure:

<div class="drill" data-ex="secdom" data-settings="mode=both&most=4&kind=both&inv=all&clef=treble,bass"></div>

## 17.5 Writing secondary dominants

The book's procedure, worked here for **V43/V in B♭ major** (the book's own example is a different chord):

1. Find the root of the chord after the slash: V in B♭ is **F**.
2. Go up a perfect 5th: **C**.
3. Build a major triad or a dominant seventh there: **C–E–G–B♭**.
4. Put it in the inversion asked for. 43 means the 5th is in the bass: **G–B♭–C–E**.

[Read 17.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/WritingSecondaryDominants.html)

<div class="drill" data-ex="secwrite" data-settings="mode=major&most=3&kind=both&inv=root"></div>

<div class="drill" data-ex="secwrite" data-settings="mode=both&most=4&kind=both&inv=all"></div>

## 17.6 Irregular resolutions

A secondary dominant does not always go to the chord it names. The book's examples, with its analysis:

- **V/V → IV**: "Yesterday", and V7/V → IV in "Forget You". IV can stand in for V in popular music.
- **V/V → ♭VII**: "I Want You to Want Me" (in A major). ♭VII also stands in for V.
- **V42/IV → V7/ii → ii**: "Baby Love" (in C major in the book's example: C7 over B♭, then A7, then Dm). The B♭ falls by half step to A as
  expected, but A is the root of a new secondary dominant instead of the third of F.
- **V7/vi → IV**: "(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay", "Imagine", and Beethoven's "Waldstein" Sonata. You can think of it as iii–IV with
  a chromatic note, or as a deceptive resolution inside the key of vi.

[Read 17.6](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/IrregularResoltionsOfSecondaryDominants.html)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## For teachers

- **Links with your settings:** open a drill's **Settings**, then **Copy a link with these settings**. Add `&lock=1` for a test, `&count=20` for a score.
- **Chords drilled:** V and V7 of every major and minor triad of the key: major ii iii IV V vi, minor III iv V VI VII. A chord made only
  of the key's notes is left out (V/IV in major, which is I; V/III and V/VI in minor, which are VII and III; V7/III in minor, which is VII7).
  This is because without a resolution they can't be told from diatonic chords. So IV is drilled only as V7/IV, and III in minor not at all.
- **Resolution:** the naming drill always shows and plays the chord's regular resolution (to the chord it names), in root position.
  Irregular resolutions (17.6) are taught by listening, not drilled.
- **Voicing:** close position above the bass. The drills are for spelling and labelling, not for voice leading.
- **Checked:** `node tests/lessons/secdom-drill.test.js` generates thousands of questions and checks each one by its own arithmetic. The
  root must be a perfect 5th above the resolution's root, the quality and figure must be right, at least one note must be chromatic, and the
  drawn notes must match the answer.
- **Videos:** the clips use the book's YouTube links and start and end times. Each title was checked against YouTube.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
